title: Bhishma waits for the sun
hookLine: the old man who could choose the hour of his death waits for the sun to turn, then goes with his eyes on Krishna
carry: at the last breath, hold God's name
tomorrow: the war is won. why can't the new king get up?

lines: WAITING FOR THE SUN TO TURN.
cards: Bhishma carries an unusual gift. Long ago, his father blessed him so that death would come only when he chose it.

So he has been lying on the arrows, teaching, and waiting for a particular turning of the year: the time when the sun begins its northward course, called uttarayana, which the tradition holds as an auspicious time to die.
He sent Yudhishthira back to the city to rule. Now the season has turned, and Yudhishthira returns to the field with fire, garlands and everything needed for the last rites.

teach.b: Bhishma opens his eyes and sees them all around him: Yudhishthira and his brothers, the blind king Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Krishna. The time has come, he says. Then he turns to Krishna and asks for leave to go.
A man who can choose his own death still asks permission to take it. Krishna gives it. And Bhishma does something the text describes almost like a meditation.
He draws his life breath inward, part by part, and as it withdraws from each limb, the arrows there fall away and the wound closes.
At last the breath leaves through the crown of his head, rising like a great light into the sky. Notice where his eyes are as he goes: on Krishna. That's a teaching Hindus still live by.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says whoever leaves the body remembering him comes to him, and the same chapter names the sun's northward months as the bright path.
It was from this bed of arrows, the epic says, that Bhishma taught the Vishnu Sahasranama, the thousand names of Vishnu that many Hindus chant today.

teach.h: HOLD GOD'S NAME AT THE END
teach.b: So at a Hindu deathbed, families often chant God's name, and place a drop of Ganga water or a tulsi leaf on the lips. Death isn't hidden or hurried. The last breath is given a direction.
Then come the rites, and the river goddess Ganga rising from the water, weeping for her son, and Krishna comforting her: he has gone to the heavens. Don't grieve.

how: Bhishma's death at uttarayana is remembered in Hindu tradition, and some communities observe a day in his memory, Bhishma Ashtami, with water offerings in his name; at a deathbed, many Hindu families chant God's name and give Ganga water or a tulsi leaf.

games.q: a friend's grandmother is near the end, and her family is chanting by the bed. your friend asks why. by Bhishma's death, what fits?
o: it's to cover the noise of the hospital.
Hindus hold the last thought matters, so they give it God's name, the way Bhishma went with his eyes on Krishna.
it's a custom with no meaning; nobody really knows.
games.why: the Gita: whoever leaves the body remembering Krishna comes to him. the chanting gives the last breath a direction.

practice: Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. On each out-breath, say a name of God quietly, the one your family uses: Ram, Krishna, Om Namo Narayanaya, Om Namah Shivaya. Let the name ride the breath out, unhurried.
If you don't pray, choose one word that steadies you and let it ride the out-breath instead.
